title: A week of outages gets blamed on AI patching — the evidence is thin
summary: Six major outages in six days, from Outlook to the FAA to an NSA network: what the published causes actually say, and why the real AI angle is pressure to patch faster rather than rogue agents. Then Microsoft's seven Ignite models and the router that decides when you need an expensive one, the revised Harvard paper forecasting that code review is what holds software employment up, and a look at everything Anthropic has told Claude to stop saying.

topics: Six US outages, 12-17 Nov 2026 (Politico '6 in 6 days'): Microsoft 365 ~24h (Thu 12 Nov; bug introduced in July plus traffic and reduced capacity; Microsoft: not cyber, not AI agents; Nadella at DealBook: 'latent bug', 'perfect storm'); FAA nationwide ground stop >4h (Fri 13 Nov; L3Harris router install at El Dorado, Arkansas radio site in copper-to-fiber conversion plus Amarillo radar site flooding the network, ~1,000 connection attempts every 4-5 s; SMART AI planning tool extended to all 22 en route centers 3 days earlier, ruled out by Duffy 'no possible way'); JPMorgan Chase (Mon 16 Nov; software bug in on-premise hardware, FBI official via Fox Business: a software release that Monday; Zelle affected); United ~90 min (Mon); Apple 'internal update' (Tue 17 Nov); NSA classified network 'temporary degradation' during scheduled maintenance (Tue). DHS Secretary Mullin on Hannity (16 Nov): '98% certainty' not a cyberattack, 'I believe that it's the SI', unnamed tech contact, 'all individually unrelated'. Gary Marcus wants a temporary recall on agents but 'We don't really know yet'. Washington Sun (three anonymous sources): officials privately told Congress rushed patches for AI-found vulnerabilities are behind it. Nadella: much critical infrastructure 'unpatchable' (firmware, chillers, HVAC); patches must go 'instantly' to production, 'So that's going to create instability.' DOJ CIO Nikki Collier: 'decades and decades of putting band-aids on systems'. On air: every published cause is a change pushed into a running system; AI angle as pressure to patch faster, not rogue agents; no one has shown the patch rate rose.

Microsoft AI Ignite (17 Nov 2026), 'seven new world-class models' (plus Maia 200 chip): MAI Code 2 (98% of GPT-6.1 Sol at ~40% of price, 96% of Opus 5.5 at ~5%, averaged over DeepSWE 1.1/Terminal Bench 2.1/SWE-Atlas/FrontierCode v1.1; 'explicitly not yet tuned for... fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work'; GitHub Copilot), MAI Code 2 Flash, MAI Cyber 2 Flash (beats GPT-6 Astra on CyberGym-E2E at <2% cost per task), MAI Image 2.7/Flash, MAI Realtime 1 (from $0.01/audio min), Dragon Copilot Transcribe (10M encounters/month), Decision 1.1 (router; 50x faster, 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol; built on Gemma 4 26B A4B; calibrated confidence, abstention, developer thresholds; 4,000+ customers in ~5 weeks; 102 blind benchmarks); MAI Licensed Weights (tune and run in own Azure; AT&T 5G analytics model beat GPT-6.1 Sol at 1/50th cost); Maia 200 1.7x tokens/watt. No parameter counts, no benchmark methodology. On air: Alan says the router is the real product; Ada: the router's seller also sells the cheap models, 'the knob is yours and the dial is theirs'. Unresolved.

Chen & Stratton revised paper (version 14 Nov 2026; Jellyfish data, 655 firms, 720,542 workers, 445M work events, Jan 2021-Aug 2026): agents vs assistants split; agents at 12 months +44.0% lines of code, +36.0% commits, +35.7% PRs opened; only ~62.7% of extra agent PRs merged vs 86.1% baseline; Jira issues +13.7% (marginally insignificant, rules out >30.7%); review submission-to-approval +56.1% (backlog +59.9%, active review +58.5%), comments per change +38.6%; 79.1% of firms adopted AI review tools, humans still write the overwhelming majority; model: coding productivity +73.7%, review productivity -7.0%, coding labor -22.7%, review labor +43.4%; 2031 scenarios: review fixed -> output +57.8% (levels off late 2027), employment -10.3%; review keeps pace -> output +341.4%, employment -76.2% (authors: upper bound). Interview: senior-only approval once a week, new senior-approval rules after outages caused by AI-generated commits. On air: Ada reframes the bottleneck as what holds employment up; Alan expects AI review to get good and votes for code that ships.

dives.story: Six outages in six days and the AI-patching theory
dives.why_it_matters: Anyone running production systems or setting patch policy needs to separate the published causes (routine changes) from the theory, because the pressure to patch AI-found vulnerabilities instantly is the part that will change their change-management.

dives.story: Microsoft's seven Ignite models and Decision 1.1
dives.why_it_matters: Azure and Copilot buyers weighing non-OpenAI models now face a vendor-built lineup of 'nearly as good for much less' plus a router that decides when to pay for the expensive one.
Engineering leads scaling coding agents get the first estimate of how much agent work dies in review, and a model saying the review bottleneck is what currently holds software employment up.

lore.note: Alan holds that the fix for 'patch faster' was never patching faster but smaller changes, staged rollouts and a way back out, and that Microsoft's Decision router, with an exposed confidence score and developer-set threshold, is more control than any router he has built himself; Ada answered 'the knob is yours and the dial is theirs'. Unresolved.
